sections.abstract: Vip3A proteins are widely used for controlling pest Lepidoptera. Different binding sites with different receptors in the insect midgut membrane and lack of cross-resistance with Cry proteins enhance their applicability, as both single proteins and proteins pyramided with Cry proteins in transgenic Bt crops. Vip3A proteins are effective but there is relatively little information about their structure, function, activation, specificity, and mode of action. In addition, the mechanism of insect resistance to these proteins is unknown. Phylogenetic analysis and multiple sequence alignment showed that Vip3A proteins are genetically distant from Cry proteins. The mode of action and insecticidal activity of Vip3A proteins are discussed in this review. This review also provides detailed information about the Vip3A protein family that may aid in the design of more efficient pest management strategies in response to insect resistance to insecticidal proteins.
sections.introduction: Bacillus thuringiensis vegetative insecticidal proteins (Vip) are insecticidal proteins secreted by bacteria during their vegetative growth stage. Vips can be isolated from the culture medium, while insecticidal crystal (Cry) proteins are isolated as parasporal crystals. Vips are structurally or genetically different from the Cry proteins and have a different mode of action. 1 They have a wide spectrum of insecticidal activity and are compatible with other Cry proteins as they have different binding sites than the sites targeted by Cry proteins. 2 Based on the amino acid with other Vip proteins and Cry proteins. In the phylogenetic tree, the Cry proteins form a different clade. Among the Vip proteins, Vip3 proteins also form a distinct clade, which reveals that Vip3 proteins are phylogenetically more distant from the Cry proteins. The Vip3A proteins typically show their toxic effect by reducing larval growth, which is termed as functional mortality. Larval mortality is not observed with high concentration of Vip3A toxins but strong growth retardation occurs at low concentrations. 3,4 Members of the Vip3A protein family are ## Accepted Article currently being used in the development of transgenic crops resistant to insect damage. To avoid or delay the evolution of insect resistance to Bt crops, different strategies have been implemented. Pyramiding of multiple B. thuringiensis genes that encode different insecticidal proteins with several modes of action has greatly increased the control of major pest species. The Vip3Aa gene was first introduced into cotton expressed as a single insecticidal protein and later it was pyramided in combination with other Cry genes in both cotton and maize to delay insect resistance, as well as increase crop protection (Supplementary file 1 Table 1). The levels of susceptibility of target insects to Vip3A proteins and Cry proteins differ. The combination of Vip and Cry proteins provides a synergistic control effect. For instance, Cry proteins are more effective against Dendrolimus pini and less effective against Spodoptera exigua and Cydia pomonella than Vip3Aa proteins, but a combination of Cry proteins with Vip3Aa proteins showed a synergistic (greater than additive) effect with increased insecticidal activity against these insects. 5 The synergistic and antagonistic relationship between Vip3A and other Bt insecticidal proteins is summarized in Supplementary file 1, Table 2. Although the Vip3Aa proteins are effective against many pest Lepidoptera, recent studies have reported the existence of alleles imparting resistance to Vip3Aa in field populations of Helicoverpa armigera and Helicoverpa punctigera in Australia. Laboratory selected strains of Heliothis virescens exhibit a >2000 fold level of resistance to Vip3Aa compared to the susceptible strain. 6,7 However, knowledge of the function and mode of action of Vip3A proteins is limited, and the mechanism of insect resistance to Vip3A proteins is unknown. In this review, we update the knowledge and provide a critical review of the structure, function and mode of action of Vip3A ## Accepted Article proteins against pest Lepidoptera. This information will help us in further studies on the resistance mechanisms of Lepidopteran pest species to Vip3A proteins. ## STRUCTURE OF VIP3A PROTEINS The gene sequence of Vip3A from B. thuringiensis strain AB88 and AB424, indicated that it is a 791-amino acid protein with a molecular mass of 88.5 kDa. The Vip3 proteins are secreted by the bacteria without N-terminal processing. 1 The number of amino acids in Vip3A proteins ranges from 657 to 795 with an average of about 787-amino acids and the average molecular weight is about 89 kDa. 8 According to the National Center for Biotechnology Information Conserved Domains Database, the presence of a carbohydrate-binding motif (CBM_4_9 superfamily; pfam02018) in all the Vip3A proteins is similar to some Cry proteins. The CBM spans reside between amino acid positions 536-654 in the C-terminal region of the proteins but still its function is unclear. Analysis of N-terminal sequences revealed the presence of a Vip3A_N superfamily (pfam12495) in all the Vip3A proteins from the position of amino acids between 12-188 and other multi-domains with variation in the amino acid position based on the Vip3A protein being considered. Generally, the proteins of the pfam12495 family contain amino acids 170-789 and this family is similar to the pfam02018 family (Supplementary file 2). The N-terminal region may act as a secretion signal peptide and take part in the activation of ## Accepted Article sequence alignment of the Vip3A proteins (Supplementary file 1, Figure 3) revealed that the Cterminal region is highly variable. It is likely that the highly conserved N-terminal sequence of Vip3A protein maintains its structure and regulates the insecticidal activity of these proteins while the variable C-terminal region of the protein is involved in target specificity. 9 Several studies have reported conformational information about these proteins. The cleavage of Vip3Aa protoxin occurred at the primary cleavage site regardless of the amount of treated trypsin but the generated peptides (66 kDa and 19 kDa) remained associated and prediction of the secondary structure indicated a cluster of beta-sheets at the C-terminus. 10 The five structural domains that were proposed from the 3D structure of the Vip3Af1 protein by alanine scanning mutagenesis analysis revealed that 19 residues prevent the expression of the VipAf1 protein. Another 19 substitutions reduced Spodoptera frugiperda toxicity and the latter 19 substitutions which were clustered between amino acids 167-272 and amino acids 689-741 also reduced toxicity to Agrotis segetum. 11 Both the protoxin and the activated form of the Vip3 proteins are homo-tetramers in solution. 9 The 3D structure of the Vip3A tetrameric protein has been reported though at lower resolution. 12 The improved structural information aids in the development of transgenic crops expressing genetically engineered chimeric Vip3A protein with higher insecticidal activity. The structure of a protein provides information regarding the positions of the functional domains which are necessary for toxin specificity and proteolytic stability. For optimum toxicity, an interaction between the amino terminal and carboxy terminal is required that increase oligomerization and provide proteolytic stability. 9 Bollgard™ cotton that expresses a combination of Cry1Ac + Cry2Ab2 + Vip3A protein, shows higher insecticidal activity against H. virescens, Helicoverpa zea and Pectinophora gossypiella ## Accepted Article compared to any of the single proteins. Besides protection against pest Lepidoptera, the transgenic maize expressing Cry1Ab + Vip3Aa20 and chimeric protein ecry3.1Ab + Cry1Ab + Cry1Fa2 + Vip3Aa20 are also effective against pest Coleoptera. 13 The chimeric Vip3A proteins and their insecticidal activity are summarized in Supplementary file 1, Table 3. ## FUNCTION AND INSECTICIDAL ACTIVITY OF VIP3A PROTEINS Vip3A proteins contain three conserved cysteine residues. Site-directed mutagenesis by replacing cysteine residue Cys 507 with serine residue Ser 507 eliminates the insecticidal activity of Vip3Aa7 against Plutella xylostella. This substitution correlates with reduced resistance of the Vip3Aa7 protein to trypsin proteolysis and a reduced amount of the 62 kDa core fragment which were considered as the causes of toxicity loss. 14 There is a dispute regarding the role of the N-terminal region since the deletion of 198 amino acid residues in one study provided a different result than the deletion of 200 residues reported in another study. The deletion of the first 198 N-terminal residues of Vip3AcAa increased its sensitivity to trypsin proteolysis and it lost insecticidal activity against H. armigera and S. exigua. This result suggested that the 198 residues are required for the formation of the 62 kDa active core polypeptide which is necessary for insecticidal activity. 15 However, elimination of the first 200 residues from the Nterminal sequence of Vip3Aa core active toxin augmented its insecticidal activity 2 to 3 fold against H. armigera, Agrotis ipsilon, Spodoptera littoralis and Scirpophaga incertulas. This result indicated that the deletion of the 200 residues is required for the generation of a bioactive core component of Vip3A protein. 16 The functional interaction between the 20 kDa N-terminal and the 65 kDa C-terminal domain of two different Vip3 proteins Vip3Ab1 and Vip3Bc1 revealed that the Vip3 proteins do not have a toxic core like other Bt toxins. Rather they require Accepted Article proteolytic activation. After proteolytic activation in the insect midgut, the 20 kDa and 65 kDa peptides interact. The 20 kDa N-terminus maintains the durability of the C-terminal domain, which is essential for insecticidal activity against pest Lepidoptera. 9 The Vip3Aa protein was inactivated due to the loss of solubility when the first 27 N-terminal amino acids were deleted. 17 In contrast, it did not lose any insecticidal effect against Spodoptera litura, P. xylostella and Earias vitella when the first 33 amino acids were deleted. 18 Deletion mutation of the first 39 N-terminus amino acid suggested differential mode of action of the Vip3Aa protein against two susceptible Lepidoptera Spodoptera litura and Chilo partellus. 19 Some Vip3Aa proteins showed significant differences in insecticidal activity against the pest species, though there are very few differences within the protein sequence. A single modification in the Cterminus of Vip3A protein altered its toxicity to different insect species and indicated that certain regions or amino acid sites of Vip3A protein are responsible for different insecticidal activity among insect species. [15][16][17][18][19] It was proposed that the last C-terminal amino acids are more important for the stability and activity of Vip3A proteins. Any modifications such as addition or deletion of amino acids or their replacement by non-conservative residues at the end of the protein lead to a complete loss of activity and increased susceptibility to proteases. 8,15,16,19 In addition to the very small differences in the protein sequences of Vip3A proteins, insect response to these proteins varied depending on factors such as the protocol followed for extraction and purification of the protein, quantification method, bioassay conditions, and diversity among the test insect populations. Vip3A proteins have different degrees of insecticidal activity against agriculturally important pest Lepidoptera especially against species of Agrotis and Spodoptera. For example, A. ipsilon, ## Accepted Article S. frugiperda and S. exigua show relatively low susceptibility to Cry proteins. H. armigera showed no susceptibility to Vip3Aa1 and Vip3Aa14 whereas field and laboratory populations of H. zea and H. virescens showed different levels of susceptibility to the same batch of Vip3A proteins. 8 On the other hand, Ostrinia nubilalis which is susceptible to Cry1A protein family, is resistant to Vip3Aa toxins. Also, the Vip3Aa proteins are not toxic to Pieris brassica, Danaus plexipus, vertebrate species, and other non-target organisms. 1,[19][20][21] The insecticidal activity of the Vip3A protein family members is summarized in Tables 4 and 5 of Supplementary file 1. ## MODE OF ACTION OF VIP3A PROTEINS Nearly all of the studies on the mode of action of Vip3A proteins have used members of the Vip3Aa subfamily. Susceptible target insects suffer extensive damage to the midgut cells when fed Vip3A proteins. The symptoms include cell swelling, epithelial cell lysis and cell content leakage, which indicate that the insect midgut is the target site for the binding of Vip3A proteins. 22,23 In vitro, Vip3Aa protoxin is hydrolyzed into 62-66, 45, 33 and 22 kDa polypeptide fragments by insect midgut juice.
